claims.text: Ford, then House Minority Leader, called in late March 1966 for congressional hearings on unidentified flying objects following the Michigan sightings and the swamp gas explanation.

claims.text: The Air Force established the University of Colorado study under contract in October 1966, six months after the hearing.

claims.source: Inference from the documented sequence April-October 1966 and the 17 December 1969 termination
claims.text: The 1966 congressional pressure produced a contracted study rather than an inquiry, and that study became the instrument of termination — the same substitution pattern later seen with the Robertson Panel and with AARO.

label: Gerald R. Ford
narrative: Gerald Ford was House Minority Leader and the congressman for Grand Rapids when hundreds of Michigan residents reported objects near Dexter and Hillsdale in March 1966 and the Air Force's consultant offered swamp gas as an explanation. Ford's constituents were furious, and he wrote to the chairmen of the House Armed Services and Science and Astronautics committees demanding hearings, saying he believed the American people were entitled to a better explanation than had been given. The House Armed Services Committee held a one-day hearing on 5 April 1966 — the first congressional hearing on the subject in nineteen years of official investigation. Its practical output was not disclosure but the Condon Committee: the Air Force, pressed by Congress, contracted the University of Colorado study six months later, which then furnished the justification for shutting the whole program down. Ford's intervention is the template for what happens when this subject reaches Congress in the legacy era — pressure produces a study, and the study produces closure. He never returned to the subject as President.
